strengths: Addresses a clearly identified and underexplored gap: prior hierarchical (hyper)graph generators (e.g., HYGENE, iterative local expansion) handle topology only, while FAHNES jointly generates topology and features for both graphs and hypergraphs.

The framework is carefully formalized with explicit definitions of coarsening/expansion/refinement operations on the bipartite representation of a hypergraph, and includes formal propositions (e.g., mean-feature aggregation minimizes MSE; OT-coupling preserves marginals and shortens paths) with proofs in the appendix.

The node-budget mechanism is a well-motivated, theoretically justified alternative to prior 'append target size to embedding' approaches, and ablations (Tables 4-5) show it consistently improves node-count accuracy and, more markedly, feature quality (ChamDist) on mesh datasets.

Minibatch OT-coupling is adapted in a principled, efficient way (restricted to structurally/feature-equivalent children within a cluster expansion), keeping computational overhead low while improving alignment; ablations show benefits especially for feature-bearing datasets.

Empirical results are broad: five featureless hypergraph benchmarks, two 3D mesh (feature) datasets, and two point-cloud/graph datasets, with the proposed method outperforming multiple baselines (HyperPA, VAE, GAN, diffusion, HYGENE) on topology metrics and beating a sequential disjoint topology-then-feature baseline substantially on Chamfer distance.

Reasonable reproducibility support: detailed appendices with algorithms (training/sampling), architecture description, hyperparameters, and a complexity analysis showing near-linear O(n+m+k) generation cost.

The graph point-cloud experiments show flat baselines (DiGress, DeFoG) running out of memory while FAHNES scales, illustrating the practical benefit of the hierarchical approach for larger structures relative to those particular baselines.
weaknesses: The claimed 'scalability to large, complex structures' is not strongly substantiated: synthetic hypergraphs have ~32-200 nodes, and mesh datasets are downsampled to only 50 vertices/100 triangles with very small training sets (144-682 samples); point clouds reach 1024 nodes but this is still modest relative to typical large-graph generation claims, and the Limitations section itself admits the method still struggles on the 'larger' ModelNet Bookshelf/Piano and point-cloud settings.

Feature generation is only validated on simple, low-dimensional continuous features (3D coordinates); the paper's motivating applications (molecular design with atom/bond types, circuit design) involve categorical or multi-modal features that are explicitly listed as future work rather than being evaluated, which weakens the significance claims made in the introduction.

For the 3D mesh feature-generation experiments, FAHNES is compared against only a single, relatively weak sequential (disjoint) baseline constructed by the authors, rather than against any existing feature-aware graph/hypergraph generative baseline (e.g., a flat diffusion or flow-matching model with features, when feasible at this small scale), limiting the strength of the 'joint generation is better' claim.

The DiGress/DeFoG comparison, used to argue superior scalability, only demonstrates OOM at the specific point-cloud scale tested; no controlled study varies graph size to show where exactly the hierarchical advantage begins, and it is unclear whether FAHNES's own degradation on ModelNet Bookshelf/Piano would also appear for graphs of comparable size to the point clouds.

OT-coupling's benefit is inconsistent across datasets/metrics (e.g., on Ego hypergraphs, disabling OT-coupling sometimes yields better Valid/NodeNum than enabling it), and no statistical significance testing accompanies the mostly overlapping confidence intervals in Tables 4-5, making it hard to assess whether the ablation differences are meaningful versus noise.

Some reported metrics have very high relative variance (e.g., ModelNet Piano NodeNum 0.846±1.009, ManifoldNet Bench NodeNum 0.060±0.149), which, combined with only 5 runs, raises questions about the robustness of the comparisons and whether the reported 'state-of-the-art' gains are reliable.

The complexity analysis in Appendix G assumes idealized behavior (kl ≤ k, ml ≤ m throughout generation) that depends on the model learning accurate edge refinement; this assumption is not empirically verified, so the claimed near-linear scaling is more of a best-case argument than a demonstrated property.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely under-explored problem: joint feature+topology generation for hierarchical hypergraph/graph models, extending prior topology-only hierarchical methods (Bergmeister et al., HYGENE).

The node-budget mechanism is a sensible and well-motivated design choice for handling uneven regional growth during hierarchical expansion, and is formalized with clear definitions (coarsening, expansion, refinement).
Comprehensive appendix with formal proofs, algorithmic pseudocode for training/sampling, complexity analysis, and many implementation details, which aids reproducibility.
Strong quantitative improvements over HYGENE and other baselines on featureless hypergraph benchmarks (SBM, Ego, Tree, ModelNet40), with 5-run variance reported for FAHNES.
Demonstrates scalability advantage: FAHNES successfully generates graph point clouds at a scale where flat models (DiGress, DeFoG) run out of memory.
weaknesses: For the featured graph point cloud experiments (Table 3), the only baselines (DiGress, DeFoG) both OOM, so there is no actual competing number to validate the state-of-the-art claim in this key application setting; the comparison table is essentially uncontested.

For 3D mesh featured hypergraph generation, the only baseline is a simple two-stage sequential ablation constructed by the authors themselves, not an existing competing method — so claims of 'state-of-the-art performance in jointly generating features and structure' are not well substantiated against the literature (e.g., variational flow matching for graphs, or DiGress at smaller mesh scale, are cited but never benchmarked).

Feature generation is only tested on simple continuous 3D coordinates; despite the introduction and related work heavily motivating molecular design (atom/bond types, rings), no categorical or multi-modal feature generation experiment is provided, leaving the central motivating use case unvalidated (acknowledged only briefly in Limitations).

The framework bundles many components (node budget, minibatch OT-coupling, spectral conditioning, perturbed expansion, graph inpainting heuristics, endpoint-parameterized flow matching), but ablations only isolate two of them (budget, OT-coupling); the marginal contribution of spectral conditioning, perturbed expansion, and inpainting rules is never measured, obscuring what actually drives the reported gains.

OT-coupling's benefit is inconsistent across ablation tables (Tables 4-5): in several cases (e.g., Tree hypergraphs Valid metric, ModelNet Piano Spectral) removing OT-coupling yields comparable or better results, weakening the paper's claim that it 'improves generative stability and quality' as a general-purpose contribution.

Datasets used for hypergraph/mesh experiments are very small (128 train / 32 val / 40 test, or even 144 train for Bench), raising concerns about the statistical reliability of reported improvements and about overfitting given the perturbed-expansion augmentation explicitly designed to combat overfitting in 'low-data regimes.'

Evaluation for meshes/point clouds relies heavily on nearest-training-sample Chamfer distance, which mostly rewards memorization/coverage of the training set rather than establishing genuine generative diversity or fidelity; no perceptual or downstream-task evaluation is provided.

Baseline results (HyperPA, VAE, GAN, Diffusion, HYGENE) are reported without variance/multiple seeds, while FAHNES reports mean ± 2·std over 5 runs, creating an asymmetric and potentially unfair comparison.

The theoretical propositions (mean minimizes MSE for cluster feature aggregation; OT-coupling preserves marginals and shortens paths) are straightforward, well-known results in disguise of new notation, and do not constitute a substantial theoretical contribution.

The paper's dense, heavily formalized notation (bipartite coarsening/expansion/refinement definitions, probabilistic factorization) makes the core intuition difficult to extract, and the writing could better foreground what is genuinely new versus adapted from prior work (Bergmeister et al., HYGENE, minibatch OT flow matching).

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine gap: prior hierarchical (hyper)graph generators (Bergmeister et al., HYGENE) handle only unfeatured topology, while flat feature-aware models (DiGress, DeFoG) do not scale. FAHNES is, to the reviewer's knowledge, the first method to jointly generate hypergraph topology and node/hyperedge features in a scalable hierarchical fashion.

The technical formulation is rigorous: the coarsening/expansion/refinement process is formally defined (Definitions 1, 4, 6), the probabilistic generative model is carefully derived via a Markovian factorization with a clear justification for merging the expansion and refinement distributions, and Proposition 3 gives a clean optimality argument for mean-feature aggregation during coarsening.

The node-budget mechanism is a well-motivated, simple, and interpretable addition over prior 'append target size to embedding' approaches, and ablations (Tables 4-5, 9-10) show it consistently helps, especially for feature quality (ChamDist).

Minibatch OT-coupling is non-trivially adapted to the hierarchical/permutation-equivariant setting, with formal marginal-preservation and shorter-path propositions (Appendix A.2) rather than just an empirical trick.

Experiments span synthetic hypergraphs (SBM, Ego, Tree), real 3D mesh hypergraphs (ModelNet40, Manifold40), and graph point clouds, with FAHNES outperforming HYGENE, HyperPA, VAE/GAN/Diffusion baselines by large margins on most metrics, and being the only method able to run on point-cloud graphs where DiGress/DeFoG both OOM.
Reproducibility is strong: detailed architecture, hyperparameters, training/sampling algorithms (Algorithms 1-5), and a complexity analysis (O(n+m+k)) are all provided in the appendix.

The limitations section is honest, acknowledging that the method still struggles at very large scale (ModelNet Bookshelf/Piano, point clouds) and only handles relatively simple continuous feature distributions.
weaknesses: Despite motivating the work heavily with molecular design and circuit applications (rings, atom/bond types, netlists), no experiments involve categorical or multi-modal features; all featured experiments use only 3D coordinates, leaving the central motivating claim about 'features critical in real-world applications' only partially validated.

Datasets are small (128 train / 32 val / 40 test for most hypergraph benchmarks, 144-682 samples for meshes), so it is unclear how well conclusions generalize to larger, more diverse corpora typical of molecular or circuit domains.

The feature-generation comparison rests on a single sequential-disjoint baseline built from the authors' own topology and feature sub-models rather than comparison against an established joint or disjoint alternative from the literature, which weakens the strength of the 'joint > sequential' claim.

The DiGress/DeFoG comparison on point clouds is uninformative for quality (both OOM at this scale), so the paper lacks any regime where FAHNES's feature+topology quality is directly compared against a strong flat baseline on the same data.

Ablation results are somewhat inconsistent — for several settings (e.g., Ego Hypergraphs Valid, Tree Valid in Table 4) removing the budget mechanism or OT-coupling occasionally yields comparable or even slightly better numbers, muddying the narrative that both components are strictly beneficial.

The presentation is dense with heavy formalism (many nested definitions/propositions) that may hinder accessibility; central practical intuitions (e.g., why budgets solve uneven growth) could be conveyed with fewer pages of notation and more illustrative discussion in the main text.

No wall-clock/memory comparison against baselines is given in the main paper despite scalability being a core claim; only asymptotic complexity is analyzed, and rough graph/hypergraph sizes used in experiments are still fairly modest (≤1024 nodes for point clouds).

strengths: Addresses a genuine and important gap: existing hierarchical graph/hypergraph generators (HSpectre, HYGENE) scale well but ignore features, while flat feature-aware models (DiGress, DeFoG, etc.) do not scale; FAHNES is presented as the first hierarchical method to jointly generate topology and features for both graphs and hypergraphs.

Technically substantive contributions beyond simple engineering: the hierarchical scale encoding provides finer per-cluster growth control than prior 'append target size' approaches, and the multi-scale graph OT coupling is a principled generalization of minibatch OT coupling to permutation-sensitive hierarchical graph settings, with accompanying propositions (marginal preservation, variance reduction) and proofs.

Extensive empirical validation across a wide range of settings: featureless hypergraphs (SBM, Ego, Tree, ModelNet), featureless graphs (SBM, Tree, Planar, Protein, Point Cloud), and genuinely featured hypergraphs/graphs (3D meshes, graph point clouds), with FAHNES achieving competitive or SOTA results and being the only method able to scale to large featured point clouds where flat baselines (DiGress, DeFoG, Flow Matching) run out of memory.

Careful ablations isolating the contribution of scale encoding and OT coupling (Table 5, Table 10-12), along with an ablation on coarsening strategy, showing both components matter, especially for feature quality.

Strong reproducibility support: detailed appendices with algorithms for training/sampling, full derivations of propositions, complexity analysis (O((n+m+k)log n)), and extensive hyperparameter/dataset documentation; code stated to be open-sourced.
Clear practical motivation via Figure 1 showing the failure mode of naive sequential topology-then-feature generation, which is used to motivate joint modeling.
weaknesses: The contribution is evolutionary rather than revolutionary: the coarsening-expansion scaffold, PPGN backbone, and much of the probabilistic framing are directly inherited from Bergmeister et al. (2024) and Gailhard et al. (2025); the core novelty is confined to scale encoding, feature-handling during coarsening/refinement, and OT coupling, which is accurately scoped but somewhat narrows the claimed 'first' contribution.

Mixed results on standard graph benchmarks: FAHNES underperforms DeFoG substantially on SBM graph validity (50.0% vs 90.0%) and is not consistently best across Table 2, weakening the claim of uniformly strong performance on non-featured graphs.

Feature generation is only demonstrated for continuous features (3D coordinates); no experiments with categorical/discrete or multi-modal features (e.g., atom types in molecules) are shown, despite this being highlighted as an important motivating application area (molecular design, circuits) in the introduction.

Several reported metrics have very large relative variances (e.g., ModelNet Bookshelf Node Num 0.135±0.276, ManifoldNet ablations with wide ±ranges), raising some concern about the stability/robustness of the method across runs, though this is at least transparently reported.

DeFoG comparisons are missing for Protein and Point Cloud unfeatured graph datasets (shown as '—'), and no baseline other than flat OOM-prone models is available for the more challenging featured point cloud datasets, limiting the strength of comparative claims in the most novel (large, featured) setting.

The overall method is fairly complex, with many interacting components (bipartite representation, clique/star expansions, coarsening with constrained cluster sizes, scale encoding recursion, flow matching, OT coupling, graph inpainting); while well documented in the appendix, this complexity may hinder reproducibility/adoption by others despite open-sourced code.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and clearly motivated gap: existing hierarchical graph/hypergraph generators (HSpectre, HYGENE) handle only topology, and the paper extends this line of work to jointly model features and structure, which is a useful practical contribution for domains like 3D meshes.
Broad experimental coverage across synthetic hypergraphs, unfeatured graph benchmarks, 3D mesh (hypergraph) datasets, and graph point clouds, with fairly extensive baselines within each category.

Ablation studies (Table 5, Appendix I.2) isolate the effect of the proposed hierarchical scale encoding and multi-scale OT coupling and show they generally help, lending some support to the design choices.

Reasonably careful theoretical treatment (Appendix A/B) formalizing the probabilistic model and giving proofs for feature-averaging optimality and variance reduction from OT coupling, plus a complexity analysis showing quasi-linear scaling.

Honest limitations section explicitly acknowledging that the method still struggles on very large graphs/hypergraphs (e.g., ModelNet Bookshelf/Piano, point clouds), and that it currently only handles continuous features.
weaknesses: The core novelty is largely a recombination of existing components (HSpectre/HYGENE coarsen-expand pipeline, Lipman et al. flow matching, Tong/Pooladian minibatch OT coupling generalized to clusters, VAR/FlowAR-style scale-wise prediction) rather than a fundamentally new mechanism; the paper's own framing ("generalizes", "extends the scale-wise autoregressive idea") underscores this incremental character.

The paper's central motivating claim—that prior joint topology+feature methods (DiGress, VFM/Eijkelboom et al., Xu et al.) don't scale—is never empirically tested directly against them on any dataset where they could still run at moderate scale; the actual featured baselines used in Tables 3–4 (sequential two-step, WGAN, plain Flow Matching, VAE on concatenated incidence matrices) are weak, ad hoc constructions rather than the state-of-the-art joint methods cited in the introduction, so the claimed necessity/superiority of joint modeling is not rigorously established against the strongest possible comparators.

On the unfeatured graph benchmarks (Table 2), where a legitimate SOTA comparison (DeFoG) does exist, FAHNES is clearly worse on SBM graphs (50.0% vs 90.0% validity) and Protein/Point Cloud lack DeFoG numbers entirely (marked "—"), undermining the claim of "competitive or state-of-the-art performance."

Despite framing around "large-scale" generation, most tested featured datasets remain modest in size (ManifoldNet meshes average ~50 nodes, training sets of 144–682 samples; point clouds ~1000-1400 nodes average), so the paper does not convincingly demonstrate the claimed scalability advantage on genuinely large, complex featured structures beyond showing baselines run out of memory.

Many reported metrics carry very large relative standard deviations (e.g., NodeNum 0.846±1.009, 3.622±1.822 for ModelNet Piano), which combined with only 5 runs weakens confidence in some comparative claims, particularly in the ablation tables where differences between configurations are sometimes within noise.

The Impact Statement is boilerplate and dismisses any need to discuss societal consequences, which is a fairly perfunctory treatment of ethics/limitations for a generative modeling paper with applications (e.g., circuit/molecular design) that plausibly warrant at least brief discussion.

Presentation is dense and notation-heavy (many overloaded symbols across coarsening/expansion/refinement definitions), which, combined with substantial content deferred to a lengthy appendix, makes the core contribution harder to assess from the main text alone.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and important gap: prior hierarchical graph/hypergraph generation methods (Bergmeister et al. 2024; Gailhard et al. 2025) only model topology, while flat feature-aware methods (DiGress, DeFoG, etc.) cannot scale; FAHNES is the first to jointly generate topology and features hierarchically for both graphs and hypergraphs.

Strong empirical demonstration of the central scalability claim: on graph point clouds (~1000+ nodes) and 3D mesh datasets, competing flat models (Flow Matching, DiGress, DeFoG) all run out of memory while FAHNES successfully generates, directly substantiating the quasi-linear complexity argument.

Solid theoretical grounding: propositions (with full proofs in the appendix) show that cluster-wise feature averaging is optimal under MSE, that the multi-scale OT coupling preserves the true marginal distributions (Prop. 2) and provably reduces target displacement variance (Prop. 3), and that scale-encoding-based masking (graph inpainting) recovers a non-trivial gradient signal that would otherwise be dominated by static-node identity mappings (Prop. 4).

Comprehensive experimental evaluation spanning five unfeatured hypergraph datasets, five unfeatured graph datasets, two featured 3D mesh (hypergraph) datasets, and two featured graph point cloud datasets, with FAHNES achieving best or near-best results on most metrics against a wide range of baselines (HYGENE, HyperPA, VAE/GAN/diffusion baselines, HSpectre, DiGress, DeFoG, BwR).

Thorough ablations isolating the contribution of scale encoding and OT coupling (Table 5, extended in appendix), plus an additional ablation on the coarsening strategy (random vs. feature-preserving vs. spectrum-preserving), which help substantiate the claimed necessity of each component.

High level of reproducibility support: detailed algorithms (coarsening sampling, training, sampling, OT coupling) are given in full pseudocode, hyperparameters are exhaustively specified per dataset in the appendix, complexity analysis is rigorous, and code is stated to be open source.
weaknesses: The presentation is extremely dense, with heavy notation (bipartite graph coarsening/expansion/refinement definitions, multiple index sets) that makes the paper difficult to parse without repeated cross-referencing to the appendix; this could hinder independent reproduction of core ideas even though pseudocode is provided.

Performance is not uniformly state-of-the-art: on the unfeatured SBM graph dataset FAHNES's Valid% (50.0) is notably lower than DeFoG's (90.0), and on several centrality-based metrics for unfeatured hypergraphs (e.g., Harmonic on Ego, SBM) FAHNES is worse than HYGENE, which somewhat tempers the "competitive or SOTA" framing in the abstract.

The baselines used for the *featured* mesh/point-cloud generation task (naive VAE/WGAN/flow-matching on concatenated incidence+feature representations, sequential two-stage generation) are relatively weak and may not have been as extensively tuned as FAHNES itself, making the comparative margin harder to interpret as a fair reflection of joint-vs-disjoint generation benefits rather than baseline undertraining.

The datasets used to demonstrate "large-scale" featured generation remain modest in absolute size (meshes coarsened to 50 vertices/100 triangles; point clouds ~1000 nodes), and the paper's own limitations section admits the method still struggles on the largest structures tested (ModelNet Bookshelf/Piano, point clouds), so the scalability claims, while directionally validated, are not yet demonstrated at a scale that would be considered large by broader graph-generation standards (e.g., tens of thousands of nodes).

The multi-scale OT coupling ablation (Table 5) shows a mixed and sometimes marginal effect (e.g., ManifoldNet Bench ChamCov actually degrades slightly with coupling turned off but ChamDist and other metrics improve inconsistently across settings), suggesting its practical significance is less clear-cut than the theoretical variance-reduction result implies.

Feature generation is restricted to continuous distributions (e.g., 3D coordinates); handling of categorical, discrete, or multi-modal hyperedge/node attributes—common in molecular or circuit-design applications mentioned as motivation in the introduction—is left entirely for future work, somewhat limiting the immediate applicability to the broader set of use cases the introduction motivates.

Training cost is high (1M steps per experiment on a single L40S GPU per dataset), and the paper does not report wall-clock training times or compare compute budgets against baselines, making it harder to assess the practical cost-benefit tradeoff of the added complexity (scale encoding, OT coupling, inpainting) versus simpler alternatives.
